findings.summary: The caption's first sentence is a bare series label with no hook — the actual hook (the temp-dir/Ctrl-C scenario) is buried in sentence two.
findings.evidence: "Part 2 of BASH TRAPS & SIGNALS. Your script creates a temp dir, then dies to Ctrl-C — and leaves the mess behind."
findings.fix: Lead with the scenario and demote the part label: "Your script creates a temp dir, then dies to Ctrl-C — and leaves the mess behind. (Part 2 of BASH TRAPS & SIGNALS.) This handbook is the full field guide to Bash traps: ..."

findings.summary: In the "Everything That Forks" flowchart, connector lines are routed straight through the `( ... )` and `$( ... )` nodes, striking through their labels.
findings.evidence: Horizontal edges from the "explicit"/"implicit" boxes cross the interiors of the two boxes labelled `( ... )` and `$( ... )`, passing over the `...` glyphs at mid-height rather than terminating at the box borders.
findings.fix: Re-layout the flowchart so edges terminate at node boundaries (or route around nodes) — e.g. give the crossing explicit→`$( )` / implicit→`( )` edges orthogonal routing with a vertical offset above the node row.

findings.summary: The page titled "The ERR Trap and set -e" never states when the ERR trap fires or shows a single `trap ... ERR` line, yet it teaches advanced ERR-handler content on top of that missing definition.
findings.evidence: Page 1 jumps from "Pipelines Hide Failures" to "ERR runs first — report `$?`, `$LINENO`, `${BASH_SOURCE[0]}`" and "`cmd || true` exempts one command from `set -e` and ERR"; the page contains no code block and no bullet stating that `trap handler ERR` fires when a command returns non-zero, nor the exemptions (conditions in `if`/`while`, operands of `&&`/`||`, negated with `!`).
findings.fix: Open page 1 with a definition block before the pipefail section: a bullet "`trap handler ERR` fires when a command returns non-zero, by the same rules as `set -e`", a bullet listing where ERR does NOT fire (`if`/`while` conditions, `&&`/`||` operands, `!`-negated commands), and the syllabus code line `set -Eeuo pipefail; trap 'echo "FAIL line $LINENO: $BASH_COMMAND (rc=$?)" >&2' ERR`.

findings.summary: The last third of page 1 teaches chapter 8's subshell material, including a fork-reset table that relies on `set -E`, which is only defined at the top of page 2.
findings.evidence: Page 1 ends with "Everything That Forks", the subshell-sources flowchart, "The Fork Reset Rule" table whose final row reads ["ERR + `set -E`","inherited"], and the callout "Why $(...) Feels Broken" — while page 2 opens with "Inheritance Switches": "`set -E` (errtrace): ERR reaches functions, `$()`, subshells".
findings.fix: Move the "Everything That Forks" heading, the subshell-sources flowchart, the fork-reset table and the "Why $(...) Feels Broken" callout to the top of page 2, ahead of "Inheritance Switches", so `set -E` is defined before the table cites it; backfill page 1 with the missing ERR definition and code.

findings.summary: The claim that an empty unquoted variable makes `rm -rf $tmpdir` wipe `/` is false — with no operand `rm` just errors out.
findings.evidence: Table row ["`rm -rf $tmpdir`","wipes `/`","quote + guard"] plus the bullet "An empty unquoted variable turns cleanup into a wipe" and the caption's "how an unquoted `$tmpdir` turns cleanup into `rm -rf /`".
findings.fix: With `tmpdir=` empty, `rm -rf $tmpdir` expands to `rm -rf` and GNU rm exits with "missing operand" (and `rm -rf /` is refused by the default `--preserve-root` since coreutils 6.9). Change the example to the forms that actually delete the wrong thing: a trailing slash or glob (`rm -rf $tmpdir/` → `rm -rf /`, `rm -rf $tmpdir/*` → `rm -rf /*`), or an unquoted path containing whitespace (`tmpdir="/tmp/my dir"` → removes `/tmp/my` and `dir`). Update the caption to match.

findings.summary: The verification step asserts exit status 143 after SIGTERM, but nothing in the handler contract re-raises TERM, so the prescribed skeleton cannot produce 143.
findings.evidence: "Run the script, `kill -TERM` it from another terminal" / "Assert the temp dir is gone and status is 143", while the only re-raise guidance is "For INT finish with `trap - INT; kill -INT \"$$\"` — callers see 130" (and page 2: "INT without re-raise" → "reports 0").
findings.fix: Generalise the re-raise rule to every catchable termination signal: in the handler do `trap - "$sig"; kill -"$sig" "$$"` (e.g. `kill -TERM "$$"` → 143, `kill -INT "$$"` → 130), or state that without re-raising TERM the script resumes after the handler and exits with `main`'s status, not 143.

findings.summary: Saying traps are "copied" into a subshell is wrong and contradicts the reset table on the same page.
findings.evidence: "Variables, traps and options are copied, not shared" — immediately followed by "caught (`trap f INT`)" → "default".
findings.fix: Bash duplicates the environment "except that traps caught by the shell are reset to the values that the shell inherited from its parent at invocation." Reword to "Variables and options are copied; caught traps are reset to default" so the bullet matches the Fork Reset Rule table.

findings.summary: The "Everything That Forks" figure renders the label "subshell sources" twice — once as a caption at the top of the dashed frame and again inside the diamond node.
findings.evidence: Italic "subshell sources" at the top of the dashed box, and "subshell sources" again inside the diamond directly below it.
findings.fix: Drop the figure caption (or the diamond's duplicate text) so the label appears once.

findings.summary: Each page carries the opening section of the next chapter, so the mistakes list starts on the subshell page and the production skeleton lands on the trade-offs page, splitting both topics across a page break.
findings.evidence: Page 2 ("Subshells: Where Traps Vanish") ends with "Four That Bite Everyone" and its table of four mistakes, while page 3 ("Trade-offs, Costs, and Failure Modes") carries the other four under "Silent Teardown Failures"; page 3 then ends with "The Skeleton" (`set -Eeuo pipefail` / `mktemp -d` / `trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM HUP`), which belongs to page 4, "Production Patterns and Summary".
findings.fix: Realign section-to-page boundaries: move "Four That Bite Everyone" and its four follow-up bullets to the head of page 3 so all eight mistakes sit together, and move "The Skeleton" code block plus its flow diagram to the head of page 4 ahead of "Handler Contract".

findings.summary: `set -m` does not make group-killing safe by making you the group leader — it makes children leaders of their own groups, which is the opposite mechanism.
findings.evidence: "Group kill is thorough but can hit the launching shell" / "Only safe once you are group leader via `set -m`".
findings.fix: With job control on, each `&` job gets its own process group, so the safe move is to kill the child's group (`kill -TERM -- -"$child_pid"`), not your own — and `kill 0` then no longer reaches those children at all. Reword to: "`set -m` puts each background job in its own process group; kill that group (`kill -- -$pid`) instead of `kill 0`, which would hit your own shell."

findings.summary: The lock-file pattern uses `exec` two pages after `exec` was taught as the thing that destroys every trap, with no note that a redirection-only `exec` does not replace the shell.
findings.evidence: Page 2 states "`exec cmd` replaces the image: no EXIT trap, no handlers"; page 4 then recommends "exec 9>/var/lock/my.lock" / "flock -n 9 || exit 1" with the comment "# fd closes on death — even on SIGKILL".
findings.fix: Add a clause to the page 4 lock bullets: "`exec` with only a redirection and no command does not replace the shell — it just opens fd 9 in the current shell, so your traps survive", or qualify the page 2 bullet as "`exec cmd` (with a command)".
